raw_case_text:
An 8-year-old girl was under observation at our dermatology outpatient clinic because of several skin lesions that had persisted for 5-6 months. Initially, the patient was diagnosed as having eczema and topical treatment was started. Over a 2-month period, the patient showed no improvement and showed the additional clinical presentations of epigastric abdominal discomfort, weakness, asthenia, occasional nausea, and vomiting and was referred to the pediatric ward. The skin lesions were present on both the legs and were tender, erythematous, nodular, with a predominantly nodular shape and without any discharge (Figure 1). Skin biopsy of the erythematous nodule revealed full thickness subcutaneous fat infiltration with lymphocytic white blood cell (panniculitis) without any evidence of vasculitis. The mentioned findings were consistent with a diagnosis of erythema nodosum. She did not have a history of musculoskeletal complaint, pharyngitis, blood transfusion, or any medications, all of which was consistent with her condition. She had no family history of chronic liver disease or any autoimmune disorders either. Physical examination revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly, without any other peripheral stigmata of liver disease. Her vital signs were stable.
The results of the laboratory tests were as follows: WBC count, 4,500 x 10(6) / lit (neutrophils: 39%, lymphocytes: 55%, and others: 6%); hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin: 10.3 g/dL, MCV: 71); platelets, 174,000/muL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 24; creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL; total bilirubin, 1.6 mg/dL and direct bilirubin, 0.4 mg/dL; serum aspartate aminotransfarase (AST) level, 348 IU/L (normal level, up to 40 IU/L); alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level, 555 IU/L (normal level, up to 40 IU/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level, 395 IU/L (normal level, up to 1800 IU/L in pediatric patients); and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level, 612 IU/L (normal level, up to 450 IU/L). The results of hemostatic screening tests (for the prothrombin time and international normalized ratio) were normal. Serum protein electrophoresis showed total protein level of 6.9 g/dL (normal range, 6.0-8.4 g/dL), albumin level of 3.6 g/dL (normal range, 3.5-5.0 g/dL), and globulin level of 2.97 g/dL (normal range, 2.3-3.5 g/dL). Her blood samples were not positive for HBs antigen, anti-HBc antibody, anti-hepatitis A virus immunoglobulin M, and anti-hepatitis C virus antibody. The results of the serological tests were negative for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Toxoplasma, and Brucella. The streptococcal anti-streptolysin O titer was not remarkable. Smears of gastric secretion and the microbial culture were negative for the tuberculin bacilli as were the results of the Koch bacillus (BK) and purified protein derivative (PPD) skin tests. The results of the serological tests for anti-staphylococcal and anti-streptococcal antibodies were also negative. The serum and urine levels of ferritin, ceruloplasmin, alpha1-antitrypsin, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase were normal. Urine analysis did not show any abnormalities, and there were no clinical and laboratory findings suggesting diabetes mellitus, thyroiditis, Graves' disease, or proliferative glomerulonephritis.
Abdominal ultrasonography showed increased liver size, with a coarse echotexture, but it did not show any evidence of portal hypertension and ascites. The results of chest computed tomography were unremarkable. Ophthalmological examination did not show any Kayser-Fleischer ring. An assessment of the immunoserological markers showed that anti-SMA was present at a titer of 1: 160, but serum ANA, anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and anti-LKM antibodies were not. The results of human leukocyte antigen typing were positive for DR3 and DR4. Other possible causes of EN were ruled out. Liver biopsy revealed lymphocytic infiltration with a mild degree of fibrosis, rosette formation, and other histopathological findings (interface hepatitis), indicating chronic autoimmune hepatitis.
The only obvious cause of skin lesions was chronic inflammation due to an autoimmune response. The patient was diagnosed as having type-1 AIH associated with EN, and a course of prednisolone with azathioprine was started in the second week. The patient scores for the diagnosis of AIH were calculated according to the International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group (IAIHG) revised scoring system. The pre-treatment IAIHG score of the patient was 19, which is a definite indicator of AIH. During the first follow-up (after 4 weeks of therapy), abdominal discomfort, weakness, asthenia, and fatigue were entirely resolved, and the skin nodules were significantly improved. Serum aminotransferase levels were near normal. The changes in the levels of serum aminotransferases during treatment have been shown in Figure 2. The skin lesions completely remitted after 3 months of treatment. We started the treatment with the prednisolone (2 mg/ kg/ d) and azathioprine (2 mg/kg/ d). The immunosuppressive therapy was tapered with the administration of prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day) and azathioprine (1 mg/kg/d) as a maintenance regimen when we found that the levels of serum aminotransferases remained normal the first follow up. Our patient is currently doing well, as indicated by the normal results of the laboratory tests and after the 6-month follow-up post-treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old girl presented with a 5-to-6-month history of persistent tender erythematous nodules on both legs and a 2-month history of epigastric discomfort, weakness, asthenia, nausea, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 8-year-old girl was followed in dermatology for 5-6 months for bilateral lower leg skin lesions initially misdiagnosed as eczema. Over the 2 months prior to pediatric ward referral, the lesions failed to improve on topical therapy and she developed epigastric abdominal discomfort, generalized weakness, asthenia, and intermittent nausea and vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior musculoskeletal complaints, pharyngitis, blood transfusions, or medication use; no family history of chronic liver disease or autoimmune disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for tender erythematous pretibial nodules, epigastric discomfort, weakness, asthenia, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting; negative for pharyngitis or arthralgia.

objective.physical_examination: Stable vital signs. Tender, erythematous, non-ulcerated nodules on bilateral lower extremities. Mild hepatosplenomegaly without peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease; normal ophthalmological slit-lamp examination without Kayser-Fleischer rings.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 4,500/uL (39% neutrophils, 55% lymphocytes, 6% other), hypochromic microcytic anemia (Hb 10.3 g/dL, MCV 71 fL), platelets 174,000/uL, ESR 24 mm/h. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 348 IU/L (normal <=40), ALT 555 IU/L (normal <=40), ALP 395 IU/L (pediatric normal <=1,800), LDH 612 IU/L (normal <=450), normal PT/INR and GGT. Serum protein electrophoresis: total protein 6.9 g/dL (normal: 6.0-8.4), albumin 3.6 g/dL (normal: 3.5-5.0), globulin 2.97 g/dL (normal: 2.3-3.5). Normal serum/urine ferritin, ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, and urinalysis. Negative HBsAg, anti-HBc, HAV-IgM, anti-HCV, CMV, EBV, Toxoplasma, Brucella, ASO, anti-staphylococcal antibodies, PPD skin test, and gastric aspirate AFB smears/cultures. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with coarse echotexture without portal hypertension or ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT unremarkable. Skin biopsy of a leg nodule revealed full-thickness septal/lobular lymphocytic panniculitis without vasculitis, diagnostic of erythema nodosum. Autoimmune panel showed positive anti-smooth muscle antibody (anti-SMA 1:160) with negative ANA, AMA, and anti-LKM antibodies; HLA typing was positive for HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4. Percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated portal lymphocytic infiltration, interface hepatitis, hepatocyte rosettes, and mild fibrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Brucellosis, viral hepatitis, Wilson disease, and tuberculosis were excluded; positive anti-SMA (1:160), HLA-DR3/DR4 positivity, liver biopsy interface hepatitis, and a revised IAIHG score of 19 confirmed definite Type 1 Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH) presenting with erythema nodosum. Treated with oral prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day, tapered to 0.5 mg/kg/day maintenance) and azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day, tapered to 1 mg/kg/day maintenance), achieving resolution of constitutional/abdominal symptoms and near-normalization of transaminases at 4 weeks, complete remission of erythema nodosum at 3 months, and sustained remission at 6-month follow-up.
